Looking for suitable Baas
### Summary

hey im a Front end dev and i use mongoDb(mongoose) aswell as NextJs + better auth and  i was wondering  if there is any suitable plug and play baas for the setup without me being forced to change the code and models (not api rout) its for an ecommerce website and im using a bank api for payment . as i know sql injection isnt a thing for mongodb and if im using better auth for authentication and im letting the bank handle the payments while keeping things server side - and im using stating a role based posting and verification so products are probably safe too cuz of better auth do i even need the baas

### Additional information

_No response_

### Example

_No response_
You don’t really need a BaaS for what you’ve described.

You already have the main components a BaaS would normally replace or abstract away:

* MongoDB + Mongoose → your database layer
* Better Auth → authentication
* Bank API → payments handled externally
* Next.js server-side routes/actions → backend logic

Most “BaaS” options (Supabase, Firebase, Appwrite, etc.) would actually **require changing your data model and auth layer**, especially since they’re not designed to work transparently with Mongoose schemas.

So in your case:

* If your system is working and you’re comfortable maintaining it → **you don’t need a BaaS**
* If you want managed infrastructure only → you already effectively have that via MongoDB Atlas + your current stack
* If you want real backend abstraction → you would need to migrate away from MongoDB/Mongoose, which sounds like what you want to avoid

Also, MongoDB is not “safe from SQL injection” by default—the risk depends on how queries are built (e.g. unsafe operators or user-controlled filters), not the database type itself.

**Conclusion:** there isn’t a plug-and-play BaaS that fits your setup without code changes, and you don’t strictly need one for an ecommerce app with your current architecture.

Next.js itself has correct support for symlinks.

If anyone wants to use symlinks in their project, you can change the calls from `.lstat(` to `.stat(` in the following file: 
```

```

Then use [patch-package](https://www.npmjs.com/package/patch-package) to create a patch for your version of Next.js:
```bash
npx patch-package next
```
And then update your `postinstall` to patch packages after install:

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/614439b9-56f8-4343-98a0-e40bd564d3d0)

The scope of this bug is relatively small: **You can symlink files and non-route directories, just not route directories.** The bug is in the development server's route manifest generation.

I don't have the time to prioritize and fix this myself, but hopefully this helps explain things if somebody does want to try to fix it.

---

I looked into this. Unfortunately, a proper fix would be a lot more complicated than modifying watchpack:
- The issue is in `packages/next/src/server/lib/router-utils/setup-dev-bundler.ts` where watchpack is called (so you're very close!).
- Watchpack *intentionally* watches the symlink and not the target. Watchpack needs to know if the symlink changes to point to a new target. If you just replace `fs.lstat` with `fs.stat`, it'll break that behavior.

Watchpack has a `followSymlinks: true` option, but it doesn't do what we want either. It ensures that both the symlink and the target are in the watched set, but it won't return the "contents" of a symlinked directory. E.g. for a directory structure like this:

```
/foo             (directory)
/foo/buzz.txt    (regular file)
/foo/bar.txt     (symlink to /bar.txt)
/foo/fizz        (symlink to /fizz)
/bar.txt         (regular file)
/fizz            (directory)
/fizz/nested.txt (regular file)
```

if you watch `/foo` with `followSymlinks: false`, your watched set will be:

```
/foo
/foo/buzz.txt
/foo/bar.txt
/foo/fizz
```

If you use `followSymlinks: true`, it'll follow those symlinks outside of the `/foo` directory:

```
/foo
/foo/buzz.txt
/foo/bar.txt
/foo/fizz
/bar.txt
/fizz
```

However, it won't watch the contents of `/fizz`. For that, we'd need some logic to simulate expanding the contents of the symlinked directory.

We can simplify things a bit by not allowing symlinks for route directories that point outside of the watched project directory/repository, but a proper solution would still be rather complicated:
- Use `readlink` on every file to try to read the contents of a symlink (if it errors with `EINVAL`, we know it's not a symlink).
- Cache the link resolution, so we only re-run it on changed files.
- If a symlink points outside of the watched directory, log a warning and don't try to follow it.
- Use the cached set of all symlinks inside the watched directory to follow all symlink chains and expand their paths. Bail out if you detect cycles.
- For expanded paths pointing to directories, copy all of their children. Rewrite the path's parent directory to be the symlink, so that the symlink "contains" these files.

If fixed, this may reveal other issues with directory traversal in other parts of Next.js.

### Summary

When the next server is running, the unix "ps" title when I'm running a few different apps at the same time:
```
% pgrep -a next-server
182 next-server (v15.5.12)
190 next-server (v14.2.35)
```

### Additional information

Hello thorfi. It is definitely possible to customize the unix process name but you cannot achieve it directly through the default CLI flags.

Next js uses the underlying Node js process title to set that name. To override it you will need to create a custom server script instead of using the standard next start command. In your root folder you can create a file named server.js and set process.title equal to whatever custom name you want right at the very top of the file.

After setting the title you can initialize the Next js server programmatically using the next function from the next module. Once you bind it to your http server and start listening on your port the unix ps command will display your custom title instead of next-server for that specific application instance.

This makes it very easy to distinguish between multiple projects running on the same machine.
This is set here: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/bdf11299c1ed96ec92735ea98c37c17448ad5de5/packages/next/src/server/lib/start-server.ts#L195

I guess, you could set an `instrumentation.ts` file, and change the `process.title` from within the register function? That should override the above?

- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/instrumentation

For when `NEXT_RUNTIME` is `nodejs`.
@thorfi I don't see an official Next.js config option for customizing the unix process name shown as 
ext-server.

Common workaround is an OS/process-manager wrapper (for example Linux exec -a ...) so process listing shows your chosen label, but that is outside Next config itself.

It's time to drop an update here.

There has been some confusion for `cacheHandler` and `cacheHandlers` usage. One thing we should state clearly is that you can use both.

In the case of OP here, the problem is serialization. As this issue points out: https://github.com/mrjasonroy/cache-components-cache-handler/pull/29

> Next.js 16 stores segmentData as a Map<string, Buffer> and rscData as a Buffer on APP_PAGE cache entries. Plain JSON.stringify converts Maps to {} and loses Buffer identity, so on deserialization segmentData.get() throws

And the solution, as the PR also points out, is to fix the serialization (and deserialization).

cacheComponents: true Server Actions on dynamic routes ([param]) return prerendered HTML shell (text/html) instead of RSC payload (text/x-component) in next start, causing "An unexpected response was received from the server
Next.js: 16.2.x
React: 19.2.0
Turbopack: enabled (default in 16)
cacheComponents: true
Deployment: Self-hosted (next start) — NOT Vercel

Describe the bug
When cacheComponents: true is enabled and a Server Action is called from a dynamic route segment (e.g. /admin/curriculum/[courseId]), the server returns content-type: text/html with the prerendered PPR shell instead of content-type: text/x-component. This causes the Next.js client to throw:
`An unexpected response was received from the server.`

This only happens when I build the project and run the production build locally....
It does NOT happen in:
next dev
Deployed to Vercel
It works fine in dev mode and  on vercel...

To Reproduce

Enable cacheComponents: true in next.config.ts
Create a dynamic route: app/admin/[courseId]/page.tsx
Place a Client Component on the page that calls a Server Action (e.g. a dialog that submits a form)
Run next build && next start
Trigger the Server Action
Observe the POST request in DevTools  response is text/html with x-nextjs-postponed: 1 and x-nextjs-prerender: 1 instead of text/x-component


Investigation findings
After next build, the .next/server/app/admin/[courseId].html file is generated  a prerendered PPR shell. When next start receives the Server Action POST to /admin/[courseId], instead of routing it to the action handler, it serves this prerendered shell, returning text/html.
The response headers on the failing POST:

```
content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8
x-nextjs-postponed: 1
x-nextjs-prerender: 1
x-nextjs-stale-time: 300

```

The .meta file for the route contains a full postponed blob baked at build time.
**Key proof  moving to a non-dynamic route fixes it:**
When the exact same page and Server Action are moved to simple route like this (e.g. app/admin/courses/page.tsx with no [param]), no .html file is generated in .next/server/app/admin/, and Server Actions work correctly. The issue is exclusively triggered by dynamic route segments with cacheComponents: true.

**Attempted workarounds that did NOT fix it:**

Adding await connection() from next/server at the top of the page  the .html shell is still generated at build time and still served for POSTs
Adding export const dynamic = "force-dynamic" incompatible with cacheComponents, throws a build warning and has no effect
Adding Supabase data fetching (cookies(), headers()) directly in the page shell is still generated
Deleting/bypassing the proxy (proxy.ts ) entirely no effect
Adding generateStaticParams returning []  no effect

**Attempted workaround that DID fix it (unacceptable for production):**

Moving the page out of the dynamic route segment into a hardcoded path stopped the .html from being generated and Server Actions started working. This confirms the issue is specifically tied to dynamic route segments + cacheComponents PPR shell generation.

Root cause hypothesis
With cacheComponents: true, PPR generates and stores a .html postponed shell for every dynamic route at build time. When next start receives a Server Action POST (identified by the next-action header), it appears to be incorrectly routing it through the PPR shell-serving path instead of the Server Action handler path.


Expected behavior
A POST request with a next-action header to a PPR dynamic route should always be handled as a Server Action and return content-type: text/x-component, regardless of whether a prerendered shell exists for that route.
Actual behavior
The prerendered .html shell is returned with content-type: text/html, breaking the Server Action entirely.


What is the fix ?
Is there a supported way to opt a specific dynamic route out of PPR shell generation with cacheComponents: true, so Server Actions on those routes work correctly in next start?
If not, this appears to be a bug in how next start dispatches POST requests to PPR dynamic routes —the next-action header should take precedence over the PPR shell path.

I noticed that there are currently two different approaches for handling `AGENTS.md` / AI docs in Next.js, and it is confusing which one should be used.

## Approach 1 — `.next-docs` at project root

Generated using:

```bash
npx @next/codemod@latest agents-md
```

This creates docs inside:

```
.next-docs/
```

This approach is mentioned here:

https://vercel.com/blog/agents-md-outperforms-skills-in-our-agent-evals#addressing-the-context-bloat-concern

This seems to be the recommended / more performant approach because it avoids context bloat.

---

## Approach 2 — Docs from `node_modules/next/dist/docs`

Generated when using:

```bash
npx create-next-app@latest
```

Docs are referenced from:

```
node_modules/next/dist/docs/
```

This approach is shown in the Next.js 16.2 AI blog post:

https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/ai-agents#existing-projects
https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16-2-ai#agent-ready-create-next-app

---

## Confusion

There are currently two different ways to provide agent docs:

- `.next-docs` directory created via codemod
- docs coming from `node_modules/next/dist/docs`

The `.next-docs` approach looks like the more performant and scalable solution, but it is not mentioned in the official Next.js 16.2 documentation.

Docs checked:

- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16-2-ai
- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/ai-agents

The `.next-docs` approach is not documented there.

---

## Questions

1. Which approach should be preferred going forward?
2. Is `.next-docs` the recommended production approach?
3. Why is the `.next-docs` approach not mentioned in the Next.js 16.2 docs?
4. Will the docs be updated to clarify this?

Clarification would help avoid confusion when setting up AI-ready Next.js projects.

The `.next-docs` folder is the result of running the codemod. Which you can use for older versions as the blog post mentions:

> On earlier versions, use the codemod to generate these files automatically: `npx @next/codemod@latest agents-md`

The recommended approach is what's documented in the 16.2 docs.

Hi all,

We're looking to setup our app as a PWA, mainly because we need some offline capabilities. I know this is a little vague of a question and probably comes down to project specifics, but, I wondered if anyone had any insight on how [next-pwa](https://www.npmjs.com/package/next-pwa) and [next-offline](https://www.npmjs.com/package/next-offline) stack up against each other?

Cheeky bump 😬
I went with `next-offline` because `next-pwa` also enables the service worker during development, which was getting really annoying for me. That also makes it very slow in development.
We are using next-offline and it is working well with a custom config. Haven't used next-pwa although but the runtime strategy looks very promising that is ideal for most web applications like NetworkFirst for /api/ and staleWhileRevalidate strategy for fonts and images, etc. 

Next-offline in general implements caching for every resource with `https://` and high limit on entries which made us fall under trap with video segments from external origins being cached leading to storage quota errors for many of the users.

I would say at the end you should always have your own strategies and patterns to cache resources which next-pwa is great at doing. If I had to use next-pwa, I would still go about having a strategy that only caches resources from my origin because it fits well to my personal use-case and caching everything is not ideal.

PPR icon (◐) shown for fully static routes when using cacheComponents
[Reference Repo](https://github.com/kWAYTV/portfolio)

The `/about` route (`apps/web/src/app/[locale]/about/page.tsx`) should be **fully static** (prerendered at build). It uses only static data and translations—no dynamic APIs, cookies, headers, or search params.

---

## Why it should be static

| Data source | Location | Dynamic? |
|-------------|----------|----------|
| `aboutCode` | `@/consts/code-content.ts` | No — hardcoded string |
| `experience` | `@/consts/experience.ts` | No — hardcoded array |
| Translations | `getTranslations("about" \| "experience")` | No — JSON files, cached |
| Locale | `params.locale` from `[locale]` | No — from `generateStaticParams` |
| OG image URL | `getPageImageUrl([locale, "about"])` | No — pure function `/og/{locale}/about/image.png` |

No `fetch()`, `cookies()`, `headers()`, `searchParams`, or DB/API calls.

---

## Data flow

```
[locale]/layout.tsx
  generateStaticParams() → [{ locale: "en" }, { locale: "es" }]
  getMessages() → from next-intl (i18n/request.ts)
  messages loaded via getCachedMessages("use cache", cacheLife)
        ↓
[locale]/about/page.tsx
  params.locale (known at build)
  aboutCode (const import)
  generateMetadata: t("title"), getPageImageUrl([locale,about])
        ↓
  AboutHeader, AboutBio, ExperienceTimeline
  getTranslations only + experience[] const
        ↓
  translations resolved at build (packages/i18n/translations/{en,es}.json)
```

---

## Structure

```
apps/web/src/
├── app/[locale]/
│   ├── layout.tsx          # generateStaticParams, setRequestLocale, getMessages
│   └── about/page.tsx      # fully static
├── components/about/
│   ├── about-header.tsx    # getTranslations only
│   ├── about-bio.tsx       # getTranslations only
│   └── experience-timeline.tsx  # getTranslations + experience[] const
├── consts/
│   ├── code-content.ts     # aboutCode (string)
│   └── experience.ts       # experience[] (array)
└── modules/i18n/
    ├── request.ts         # getRequestConfig — "use cache", cacheLife("max")
    ├── routing.ts         # localePrefix: "as-needed", localeDetection: false
    └── static.ts          # getStaticParams → [{ locale }] per config
```

---

## Expected static behavior

- **Layout**: `generateStaticParams` pregenerates one HTML per locale (e.g. `/en`, `/es`).
- **i18n**: `requestLocale` comes only from the `[locale]` segment (no cookie fallback per `request.ts`).
- **Messages**: `getMessagesForLocale` uses `"use cache"` and `cacheLife("max")` — fully cacheable at build.
- **About page**: Only params, translations, and constants—no dynamic APIs.

```
export const dynamic = 'force-static';
```
This doesn't work or what?
IIRC what's happening here is that, you can still navigate to another locale not defined in your `generateStaticParams`, and there's a static shell for that, even if empty, even if you'll just 404 it. AKA, `param` are also runtime, the set of params not defined in `generateStaticParams`.

Because the grouping in the file tree printout, is by file system route, your routes that DID complete and are fully static, are listed visually under a PPR ◐ parent, even the empty static shell (in your case there's no fallback for unknown runtime params) is listed right under the file system route name.

- You already reject unknown locales.
- If there was any further dynamic/runtime data access further down, that did not produce a fallback, the build/dev time would error. 

So you know your route + locales at build time, are completing a fully static HTML page. If you think about it, in Cache Components, the hybrid model, means that, all pages one way or another, produce a static asset, and at the same time, are able to stream data to fill in fallbacks, if necessary. That being said, I think we likely need to incrementally improve that tree printout in some way. 

The build tree printout is the way devs confirmed, whether or not our changes had introduced a subtle fetch/cookie, etc that opted out of static rendering etc... in Cache Components, you get this info directly as  you develop, or during build time, because it won't complete.

Link prefetch does not work in my app and cannot create minimul reproduction
### Summary

My application uses Next.js's static export.
It worked fine with Next.js 15, but after upgrading to Next.js 16, page transitions stopped working correctly.

- GitHub repo: https://github.com/na-trium-144/falling-nikochan/tree/next16-rsc-bug
In this repository, `frontend` workspace is a Next.js project.
- Preview deployed to vercel: https://falling-nikochan-3lao9gvpe-natrium144s-projects.vercel.app/en
- A working preview built with Next.js 15 (with some differences like the addition of onClick handler to the Link for animation): https://falling-nikochan-3y8iv0tsl-natrium144s-projects.vercel.app/en
  - Corresponding GitHub Commit [330a68a](https://github.com/na-trium-144/falling-nikochan/tree/330a68af2de9c76d4579b6f69bd481f33ccfc2b2) 

In this app, the homepage (/en or /ja) has links to pages like /en/main/play and /en/main/edit.

In Next.js 15, when the homepage was opened, it made GET requests to `play.txt?rsc=2d76s`, `edit.txt?rsc=2d76s`, etc., and clicking them would navigate to the corresponding page.

In a Next.js 16 build that isn't working correctly, when the page loads, it makes
- HEAD requests to `/en/main/play`, `/en/main/edit`, etc. (200 OK, empty response body)
- GET requests to `play/__next._tree.txt?_rsc=eqsiv`, `edit/__next._tree.txt?_rsc=eqsiv`, etc. (200 OK), and 
- GET requests to `/en/main/play?_rsc=1075s`, `/en/main/edit?_rsc=jsf70`, etc. (200 OK, returns HTML files because they lack extensions).

Clicking a link in this state results in no action, and no error messages are displayed in the console.

I suspected that fetching HTML for prefetch was incorrect and that `play.txt` or `edit.txt` should be fetched instead. 
I created a custom HTTP server that returns a `.txt` file with the same name instead of an HTML file when the query parameter has `_rsc`, and in that case the page transitions worked without any problems.
However, when deploying to the production, I want to host the output files on a CDN rather than using my own HTTP server.
I can't make CDNs (for example, Vercel) return a txt file instead of a static html file when the query parameter contains _rsc.
The documentation of vercel.json (https://vercel.com/docs/project-configuration/vercel-json#rewrites) states:

> The `source` property should **NOT** be a file because precedence is given to the filesystem prior to rewrites being applied. Instead, you should rename your static file or Vercel Function.

I tried this, but it indeed didn't work (it returned an html file for the request `play?_rsc=12345` regardless of rewrite config).

I thought about creating a minimal reproduction and starting an issue, but the prefetch behavior in the newly created Next.js 16 project was different again.
I created `/foo/page.tsx` and a link to `/foo` in the new project created with create-next-app and built it with output: "export". When I opened that page, it prefetched 
- `/foo/__next._tree.txt`
- `/foo/__next._head.txt`
- `/foo/__next._index.txt`
- `/foo/__next.foo.txt`, and
- `/foo/__next.foo.__PAGE__.txt`

Clicking the link to `/foo` then navigated to `/foo`.

Therefore, my questions are:
1. Why does a newly created project prefetch five txt files, while my app only fetches `__next._tree.txt` and the HTML file itself?
2. Is it a Next.js bug that the prefetch request is made without an extension, resulting in the retrieval of HTML instead of a `.txt` file?

My app's source code is available at https://github.com/na-trium-144/falling-nikochan/tree/next16-rsc-bug.
To make reproduction as easy as possible, I've reduced irrelevant postbuild scripts and webpack plugins, and made it buildable without environment variables.

I believe you can reproduce this using the following steps.
```
git clone https://github.com/na-trium-144/falling-nikochan
cd falling-nikochan
git switch next16-rsc-bug
pnpm install
pnpm run nbuild
pnpm dlx serve ./frontend/out/
```
And access http://localhost:3000/en.

### Additional information

```js
Operating System:
  Platform: darwin
  Arch: arm64
  Version: Darwin Kernel Version 25.3.0: Wed Jan 28 20:53:01 PST 2026; root:xnu-12377.81.4~5/RELEASE_ARM64_T8103
  Available memory (MB): 16384
  Available CPU cores: 8
Binaries:
  Node: 22.16.0
  npm: 10.9.2
  Yarn: N/A
  pnpm: 10.28.1
Relevant Packages:
  next: 16.2.2 // Latest available version is detected (16.2.2).
  eslint-config-next: N/A
  react: 19.2.4
  react-dom: 19.2.4
  typescript: 5.9.3
Next.js Config:
  output: export
```


### Example

_No response_


###Answer no 1: 

Next.js 16 introduced per-segment prefetching, where the client issues individual requests for each segment in the route tree. In this model, the client first fetches `__next._tree.txt` to discover the full segment topology of the target route, and then issues follow-up requests for each individual segment file (`__next._head.txt`, `__next._index.txt`, `__next.<segment>.txt`, `__next.<segment>.__PAGE__.txt`).

In a fresh `create-next-app` project those follow-up files exist at the paths the client constructs, so all five requests succeed and navigation works. In **your** app they don't — the `__next._tree.txt` fetch succeeds (200 OK), but all the subsequent per-segment fetches return 404 because the files on disk are at nested directory paths like `__next/play/__PAGE__.txt`, while the client router constructs **flat, dot-separated** URLs like `__next.play.__PAGE__.txt`.

When those segment fetches 404, the router's prefetch is considered incomplete. At that point it falls back to fetching the bare page URL with `?_rsc=...` appended — **without a `.txt` extension** — which on a static CDN or `serve` simply returns the `.html` file. The router receives HTML where it expected an RSC binary payload, discards it silently, and marks the prefetch as failed. Clicking the `<Link>` then does nothing because the router never resolved a valid prefetched state for that route.

The reason a new project works and yours doesn't comes down to **route complexity and path depth**. A simple `create-next-app` with `/foo/page.tsx` generates segment files whose paths happen to round-trip correctly through the build on macOS/Linux. Your app has a deeper locale-prefixed route structure (`/en/main/play`, `/en/main/edit`) that exposes the mismatch more severely — or your build has a different combination of layouts/segments that causes the path construction to diverge.

---

### Answer  no 2:

**Yes, this is a confirmed Next.js 16 bug.**

The root cause is a mismatch between the on-disk generated files and the URL paths requested during the prefetch:

| Layer | Path format |
|---|---|
| Build output (on-disk) | `__next/play/__PAGE__.txt` ← nested directories |
| Client router (browser request) | `__next.play.__PAGE__.txt` ← flat dot-separated filename |

The `output:export` copy function uses only slash (`/`) as path characters, but the path construction logic in `segment-value-encoding.ts` diverges from the actual filesystem layout for nested route structures — this manifests on **macOS/Linux too**, not just Windows, when routes are nested beyond a certain depth (as your locale-prefixed `/en/main/play` structure demonstrates).

Your diagnosis is exactly right: your custom HTTP server intercepting `?_rsc=` and serving the `.txt` file worked precisely because it patched the missing URL-to-file mapping that Next.js's static export fails to set up correctly.

The Vercel rewrite approach cannot work either — static files take precedence over rewrites on Vercel, so the `.html` file is always served before the rewrite rule fires. This is a fundamental CDN constraint, not a Vercel-specific one.

---

### Workaround 1 — Build Adapter (works on all Next.js 16.x versions)

Until [PR #86948](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/86948) lands, use the **Next.js 16 Build Adapter** to rename the on-disk files to match what the client router actually requests.

Create `build/adapter.js`:
```js
const fs = require("fs");
const path = require("path");

/** @type {import("next").NextAdapter} */
const adapter = {
  name: "fix-issue-85374",
  async onBuildComplete({ outputs }) {
    for (const file of outputs.staticFiles) {
      const targetPath = fixupPath(file.filePath);
      if (targetPath) {
        await fs.promises.mkdir(path.dirname(targetPath), { recursive: true });
        await fs.promises.rename(file.filePath, targetPath);
      }
    }
  }
};

function fixupPath(filePath) {
  const components = filePath.split(path.sep);
  const idx = components.findIndex(x => x.startsWith("__next."));
  if (idx >= 0 && idx < components.length - 1) {
    const result = components.slice(0, idx);
    result.push(components.slice(idx).join("."));
    return result.join(path.sep);
  }
  return null;
}

module.exports = adapter;
```

Then reference it from `next.config.ts`:
```ts
const config: NextConfig = {
  output: "export",
  experimental: {
    adapterPath: require.resolve("./build/adapter.js"),
  },
};
```

This flattens `__next/play/__PAGE__.txt` → `__next.play.__PAGE__.txt` after the build, making the on-disk layout match what the client router requests — so all five segment files resolve correctly on any static CDN including Vercel.

---

### Workaround 2 — `prefetchInlining` (Next.js 16.2+ only)

If you are on Next.js 16.2+, the new `experimental.prefetchInlining` option sidesteps the path mismatch entirely by collapsing all per-segment fetches into a **single inlined response per link**:
```ts
const config: NextConfig = {
  output: "export",
  experimental: {
    prefetchInlining: true,
  },
};
```

The trade-off is that shared layout data is duplicated per-link rather than cached and reused across sibling routes — but for a CDN-hosted static export it eliminates the broken multi-file resolution completely and is the lowest-friction fix if you're already on 16.2.
actually I can reproduce this in freshly created app, so long as the `Link` component has its `prefetch` prop set to `true` (as opposed to `null`/`'auto'`)

https://github.com/mdj-uk/static-export-prefetch-bug

- `pnpm dlx serve out`

Hi @na-trium-144! This issue is a classic discrepancy in how the Flight Router resolves RSC (React Server Component) payloads in static environments after a major version upgrade.

The reason your fresh project works while the upgraded one doesn't—specifically why it's fetching extensionless paths that return HTML instead of .txt files—is usually tied to a stale build manifest or a mismatch in the trailingSlash configuration that affects how the router maps assets in output: 'export' mode.

The Definitive Fix
To resolve this and ensure the router correctly identifies the .txt RSC payloads, please follow these steps:

1. Align next.config.js
In Next.js 16, the static export logic is more sensitive to the trailingSlash setting. Ensure your configuration explicitly defines this to match your hosting environment's behavior (Vercel/CDN).

```JavaScript
/** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */
const nextConfig = {
  output: 'export',
  // Ensure this is explicitly set. 
  // 'false' is usually preferred for cleaner asset resolution in static exports.
  trailingSlash: false, 
  // Optional: helps if you have complex rewrite rules in vercel.json
  skipTrailingSlashRedirect: true, 
};
```

export default nextConfig;
2. Deep Clean Build Artifacts
Upgrading from v15 to v16 often leaves stale metadata in the .next folder that isn't always cleared by a standard build. This is the most common reason why "fresh" projects work but "upgraded" ones fail. Run a full purge:

```Bash
# Remove cache, build artifacts and lockfiles to ensure a clean slate
rm -rf .next node_modules pnpm-lock.yaml && pnpm install && pnpm run nbuild
```

3. Verify Peer Dependencies (React 19+)
Next.js 16 relies heavily on specific React 19/20 internals for the router. Check your package.json and ensure you aren't using a specific React RC or experimental version that differs from what create-next-app provides in your fresh reproduction.

Technical Insight: Why this happens
In a static export, Next.js generates an app-build-manifest.json. This file tells the client-side router: "For the /play route, the data is at /play.txt".

When the upgrade is "dirty" (due to cache) or the trailingSlash config is ambiguous, the router fails to find the correct entry in the manifest and falls back to a standard fetch to the route itself. Since the CDN sees a request for /play, it serves play.html. The router then receives HTML when it expected RSC data, causing the "no action" behavior you observed.

By forcing a clean build and explicit config, the router will correctly append the .txt extension to your prefetch requests as seen in your fresh project.

Page-level vs function-level vs component-level caching, how does Next.js handle rendering?
Hi! I have a page where all parts are static except one data-fetching function, `getProjects()`. Projects don't update often, so I want to apply caching. But I'm unsure about the right level to cache at, and I have a few questions.

**Current setup:**

`page.tsx`
```tsx
export default async function Home() {
  const projects = await getProjects();
  return (...)
}
``` 

`projects.tsx` (Server Component, receives data as prop)
```tsx
export function Projects({ projects }: { projects: ProjectsQueryResult }) {
  return (...)
}
```

`getProjects.ts`
```tsx
export async function getProjects() {
  "use cache";
  cacheLife("hours");
  // fetch from Sanity
}
```

**My questions:**

1. When `getProjects()` has `"use cache"` but the page itself doesn't — does Next.js still re-render the page on every request (just using the cached data), or does the page output get cached too?

2. If I move the `getProjects()` call into the `Projects` component itself instead of calling it in the page and passing it down as a prop, will the page still re-render on every request with the same cached data?

3. What's the right level to cache at if I want the **entire page** to be static and only regenerate once per hour — page level, component level, or function level?

Thanks!

In Next.js with the App Router, the "level" of caching determines what work is saved. Since you are using the `"use cache"` directive (introduced in the [Canary and experimental versions](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache)), here is how the rendering behavior changes based on your setup.

### 1. Function-level Caching vs. Page Rendering
If you use `"use cache"` inside `getProjects()`, Next.js caches the **result** of that specific function. 

*   **Behavior:** During a request, Next.js still "runs" the `Home()` page component. However, when it reaches `await getProjects()`, it retrieves the data from the cache instead of hitting Sanity. 
*   **Result:** The page is considered **Dynamic** (rendered at request time) but it executes very fast because the data fetching is skipped. The HTML output of the page itself is not cached in the CDN/Data Cache unless the entire route is static.

### 2. Moving the call to the Component level
Moving the call into the `Projects` component allows for **Request Waterfalls** or **Streaming**, but it doesn't automatically make the page static.

*   If `Projects` is a Server Component and uses `"use cache"`, the output of that component is cached. 
*   If the rest of the page contains dynamic functions (like `cookies()` or `headers()`), the page remains dynamic. 
*   If the rest of the page is static, Next.js will attempt to prerender the page at build time.

### 3. Achieving a fully Static Page
To make the **entire page** static and regenerate every hour, you should apply the caching at the entry point or ensure the route satisfies the requirements for Static Site Generation (SSG).

| Strategy | Implementation | Effect |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Route Level** | `export const revalidate = 3600` | The entire HTML output is cached for 1 hour. |
| **Component Level** | `"use cache"` inside `<Projects />` | The component's rendered output (JSX) is cached. |
| **Function Level** | `"use cache"` inside `getProjects()` | Only the raw data from Sanity is cached. |

> [!TIP]
> For the best performance, apply `"use cache"` at the **Component level** (the `Projects` component). This caches the rendered JSX, meaning Next.js doesn't even have to perform the React rendering logic for that section of the page; it just serves the cached fragment.

If you want the whole page to be a static shell that updates every hour, use the segment config at the top of `page.tsx`:

```tsx
// page.tsx
export const revalidate = 3600; // Revalidate the whole page every hour

export default async function Home() {
  const projects = await getProjects();
  return <Projects projects={projects} />
}
```

Does your page rely on any dynamic functions like `searchParams` or `cookies` that might be forcing it into dynamic rendering?
The way to think about this with Cache Components, is that pages are no longer either static or dynamic, they can be both.

If a page is not accessing dynamic data (fetch, remote db queries, async file system reads), runtime data (cookies, searchParams, etc), or non-deterministic operations (Math.random or Date access), then it will complete its rendering, and be a fully static page. You wouldn't need to add a caching directive at all. 

This is the static shell, the static output (contribution) for this page, and in the case above, it is the entire page. This would page have zero fallbacks for dynamic content, (it contributes with zero dynamic content).

The so called dynamic data, may be cached, given some conditions, the framework shows helpful errors if you are not meeting these conditions but essentially, don't access runtime data, under a cached scope, read it outside and pass it as a function input. Don't read cookies as part of a cached function, directly or indirectly.

When dynamic data is cached, it can be included into the static shell/output. And it is given a cacheLife (implicitly 'default'). This sets the conditions for when the cached function will be executed again, in this case, that'll also update the static output. A very sort cacheLife, zero revalidate or expire under 5 minutes, is excluded from the static shell.

Anyway, to keep things short, in your case, an otherwise static page, with a fetch `getProjects`, can safely cache the fetcher only. This will generate a static page, that'll be revalidated, or expired, as given by the cacheLife profile used. Where to put the cache function is up to you, you might find it easier to keep directives and such closer to Next.js primitives (layout/page files), or prefer to isolate this to the fetching operations. 

- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife
- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/caching#putting-it-all-together

[Turbopack] Windows `next build` fails in standalone mode with `EINVAL: invalid argument, copyfile .
### Summary

### Summary
When running `next build` with `output: "standalone"` on Windows using Turbopack (default in Next.js 16+ or explicitly enabled), the build fails during the file copying phase.

It attempts to copy a traced file for the `node:inspector` module, but the destination filename contains a colon (`:`), which is invalid on Windows filesystems.

This issue persists even in **Next.js 16.1.6**, despite PR #88273 (escape colon in output names) being merged.

### Reproduction Steps
1. Create a Next.js 16.1.6 project on Windows.
2. Enable `output: "standalone"` in `next.config.ts`.
4. Run `next build`.

### Error Log
```
> Build error occurred
Error: EINVAL: invalid argument, copyfile 'D:\path\to\.next\server\chunks\[externals]_node:inspector_7a4283c6._.js' -> 'D:\path\to\.next\standalone\apps\web\.next\server\chunks\[externals]_node:inspector_7a4283c6._.js'
    at ignore-listed frames {
  errno: -4071,
  code: 'EINVAL',
  syscall: 'copyfile',
  path: 'D:\\path\\to\\.next\\server\\chunks\\[externals]_node:inspector_7a4283c6._.js',
  dest: 'D:\\path\\to\\.next\\standalone\\apps\\web\\.next\\server\\chunks\\[externals]_node:inspector_7a4283c6._.js'
}
```

### Environment
- **OS**: Windows (10/11)
- **Next.js**: 16.1.6
- **Package Manager**: pnpm
- **Turbopack**: Enabled

### Additional information

_No response_

### Example

_No response_
https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/88273 is still canary only. Try with next@canary to verify.

> earliest canary was 16.1.1-canary.19

With the release of 16.2, this is now fixed on stable.
**Update: This is fixed in Next.js 16.2.0 (stable), released March 18, 2026.**

The fix from PR [#88273](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/88273) (which escapes colons in Turbopack output filenames — required for Windows filesystem compatibility) has landed in the stable `16.2.0` release. The latest stable is currently `16.2.1`.

**To fix this, upgrade to Next.js 16.2.x:**

```bash
npm install next@latest
# or
pnpm add next@latest
# or
yarn add next@latest
```

---

**Root Cause Summary:**

When using Turbopack's standalone output mode on Windows, the build traces the `node:inspector` built-in module. Turbopack used the raw module specifier (including the colon) as part of the chunk filename, e.g.:

```
[externals]_node:inspector_7a4283c6._.js
```

Colons (`:`) are not valid in Windows file/path names, causing `EINVAL` during the file copy phase of the standalone build. PR #88273 fixed this by escaping colons in output filenames in the Turbopack file tracer.

---

**Workaround (if you can't upgrade yet):**

If you're stuck on Next.js 16.1.x and cannot upgrade immediately, you can temporarily switch back to webpack by disabling Turbopack in your `next.config.ts`:

```ts
// next.config.ts
const nextConfig = {
  output: 'standalone',
  // Temporarily disable Turbopack until you can upgrade to 16.2.x
  experimental: {
    turbopack: false,
  },
};

export default nextConfig;
```

Note: In Next.js 16+, Turbopack is the default, so you need to explicitly opt out if you want webpack builds.

Upgrading to `16.2.0+` is the recommended long-term solution.

The error is a **TypeScript compile-time error** — TypeScript is checking `site.ts` (or the active config) for the `ConatctUS` export at build time, and it doesn't find it because the second tenant's config doesn't export that component.

Here's the proper way to handle this pattern in a multi-tenant Next.js app:

## Root Cause

When you write:
```ts
import { ConatctUS } from '@/config/site'
```
TypeScript statically checks the types of `@/config/site` at compile time. If the second tenant's `site.ts` doesn't export `ConatctUS`, this is a type error — even if at runtime the right file gets used.

## Solution: Make the export optional in your config type

Define a shared interface where tenant-specific components are optional:

```typescript
// config/site.ts (shared type definition)
export interface SiteConfig {
  name: string;
  // Optional — only some tenants have this page
  ConatctUS?: React.ComponentType;
  // ... other optional components
}
```

Then in each tenant's config:

```typescript
// config/site.capturetrip.ts
import { ContactUsPage } from '@/sites/capturetrip/ContactUs';

export const siteConfig: SiteConfig = {
  name: 'CaptureTrip',
  ConatctUS: ContactUsPage, // ✅ has it
};

// config/site.holiday2cherish.ts
export const siteConfig: SiteConfig = {
  name: 'Holiday2Cherish',
  // ConatctUS not included — that's fine, it's optional
};
```

## Usage in the page — check before rendering

```tsx
// app/contact/page.tsx
import { siteConfig } from '@/config/site';
import NotFound from 'app/not-found';

export default function ContactPage() {
  const { ConatctUS } = siteConfig;

  if (!ConatctUS) {
    return <NotFound />; // Show 404 for tenants without this page
  }

  return <ConatctUS />;
}
```

Since `ConatctUS` is typed as `React.ComponentType | undefined`, TypeScript will require you to check for it before rendering — which is exactly what you want.

## Alternative: `next/dynamic` with a fallback

If you want to load the component lazily:

```tsx
import dynamic from 'next/dynamic';
import NotFound from 'app/not-found';

// Only load the component for tenants that have it
const ConatctUS = siteConfig.ConatctUS
  ? dynamic(() => Promise.resolve(siteConfig.ConatctUS!))
  : null;

export default function ContactPage() {
  if (!ConatctUS) return <NotFound />;
  return <ConatctUS />;
}
```

## Summary

The fix has two parts:
1. **Type-level**: Define optional component properties in your `SiteConfig` interface so TypeScript doesn't complain when a tenant doesn't have it
2. **Runtime-level**: Check `if (!ConatctUS)` before rendering and return `<NotFound />` when the component is absent

This is the standard pattern for multi-tenant apps where not every tenant has the same set of pages/components.

documents.text: Next.js recommended install shows 9 moderate vulnerabilities I initialized a new Next.js project using the `recommended setup`, and the installation reported multiple moderate severity vulnerabilities. I think it is just one vulnerability, https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f886-m6hf-6m8v, it is just discoverable through other paths. If you had done pnpm audit, you'd see something like: ``` ➜ pnpm audit ┌─────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ moderate │ brace-expansion: Zero-step sequence causes process │ │ │ hang and memory exhaustion │ ├─────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ Package │ brace-expansion │ ├─────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ Vulnerable versions │ <5.0.5 │ ├─────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ Patched versions │ >=5.0.5 │ ├─────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ Paths │ .>eslint>minimatch>brace-expansion │ ├─────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ More info │ https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f886-m6hf-6m8v │ └─────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ 1 vulnerabilities found Severity: 1 moderate ``` In both cases you can do `--production` too, and that confirms that this is a dev time issue only. Looks like brace-expansion disclosed a vulnerability a few days ago. This is completely normal and nothing to worry about! Here's why: The npm audit vulnerabilities you see after create-next-app are almost always in dev dependencies (like bundlers, linters, or testing tools) — not in your actual production code that runs for users. A few things to know: Check if they're in production deps — Run npm audit --omit=dev. If no vulnerabilities show up, they're only in dev tools and pose no real risk to your deployed app. Next.js team is aware — These are typically transitive dependencies (dependencies of dependencies). The Next.js team regularly updates them, so keeping Next.js updated with npm install next@latest usually resolves them over time. Don't blindly run npm audit fix --force — This can break your app by installing incompatible versions. Only fix vulnerabilities that npm audit marks as affecting production. Context matters — "Moderate" severity in a dev tool used only on your local machine is very different from a vulnerability in code that handles user data in production. In short: if npm audit --omit=dev comes back clean, you're good to deploy!

### Summary

I’m using Next.js 16 with the new React Compiler but I also use Lingui macros.
Since Lingui needs to be processed before React Compiler, I’m trying to figure out how to make SWC or Babel run the Lingui transformation first — otherwise, React Compiler breaks Lingui macros.

### Additional information

```js
Operating System:
  Platform: darwin
  Arch: arm64
  Version: Darwin Kernel Version 25.0.0: Wed Sep 17 21:41:39 PDT 2025; root:xnu-12377.1.9~141/RELEASE_ARM64_T8103

```

The problem is that Next.js 16's `reactCompiler: true` flag doesn't currently allow you to control this plugin order, as it manages the compiler internally (and likely runs it first, per the React team's general rule).

To fix this, you must force Next.js to use a custom Babel configuration by removing the `reactCompiler: true` flag, and creating a .babelrc file. This will use Babel for compilation (which is slower than the default SWC-only path) but gives you the control you need.

Create this .babelrc file in your project's root:
```JSON
// .babelrc
{
  "presets": ["next/babel"],
  "plugins": [
    "@lingui/babel-plugin-lingui-macro", // Must be first
    "babel-plugin-react-compiler"        // Runs after Lingui
  ]
}
```

This configuration respects Lingui's requirement and should solve the issue where macros are breaking.

Also, you can check [docs](https://nextjs.org/docs/pages/guides/babel) on how to setup babel.

documents.text: Does a Next.js SPA always end up with CSP-violating code? ### Summary Our team is currently evaluating migrating our legacy SPA from Webpack to Next.js. After scaffolding a minimal project using the official documentation and configuring it for Static SPA (SSG) output. Ref: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/installation#quick-start https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/single-page-applications#static-export-optional SOP 1.npx create-next-app@latest my-app --yes 2.modify next.config.ts by just add "output: 'export'," -- We encountered the following error upon deployment. It appears to be related to native Next.js syntax. Is this an unavoidable issue when using this stack?" our csp header setting example: default-src 'self' https://*.exampledomain; script-src 'self' https://*.exampledomain ; img-src 'self' data: https:; object-src 'none'; Reproduce code: [my-app.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/26177325/my-app.zip) ### Additional information _No response_ ### Example https://github.com/gmiloveyou/TestNextJsTemplate Could you upload the app to codesandbox or a github repository to inspect there? Thanks. Yes, this is an unavoidable characteristic of Next.js — it always injects inline scripts that require special CSP handling. **What Next.js injects** Even with `output: 'export'`, Next.js includes inline `' "$f" | ... done ``` Some teams use tools like [csp-hash-generator](https://report-uri.com/home/hash) or write a post-build script to handle this. **Option 2: `'strict-dynamic'` (recommended for SPAs)** If you're deploying to a server (not pure static file serving), the `'strict-dynamic'` keyword is the modern approach. It lets a trusted script dynamically load other scripts without needing inline permissions. Combined with your deploy server adding a nonce, this works well — but it requires switching from `output: 'export'` to standard Next.js server mode. **Option 3: `'unsafe-inline'` (pragmatic)** For internal tools or environments where the threat model allows it: ``` script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' https://*.exampledomain; ``` This is the most common approach for SPA deployments that need quick CSP adoption. **Option 4: Migrate to Next.js server mode with nonces** Next.js has first-class nonce support for App Router in server mode. This is the cleanest CSP solution but requires a server: ```ts // middleware.ts import { NextResponse } from 'next/server' export function middleware(request: Request) { const nonce = Buffer.from(crypto.randomUUID()).toString('base64') const response = NextResponse.next() response.headers.set( 'Content-Security-Policy', `script-src 'self' 'nonce-${nonce}' 'strict-dynamic'; ...` ) return response } ``` The [Next.js CSP docs](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/content-security-policy) cover this in detail. --- **Short answer:** no, you can't fully avoid inline scripts with Next.js static export today. For production use with strict CSP, the hash-based or `'strict-dynamic'` + server approach is the way to go.

What is the difficult point of Redux and Context in React.js?

Difficult points of Redux
Redux is powerful, but beginners find it hard because:
Too much setup 
You need actions, reducers, store, dispatch… many files and concepts.
Hard to understand data flow 
State changes only in one direction → action → reducer → store → UI.
Boilerplate code 
Writing a lot of code even for small features.
Redux is best for large apps with complex shared state.

Difficult points of React Context
Context is simpler than Redux, but it also has problems:
Re-render issues 
When context value changes, all components using it re-render.
Not good for complex state logic 
Handling many updates, async logic, or big state gets messy.
Hard to manage multiple contexts 
Using many contexts can make the app structure confusing.
Context is best for small or simple global state (theme, auth user, language).

Dev mode: blank page when SSR error + HMR WebSocket fails (debugChannel blocks hydration) ## Summary When a server component throws during SSR in dev mode, Next.js falls back to client-side rendering via the `error.tsx` boundary. This works on `localhost`, but produces a **permanently blank page** when accessed via any non-localhost address (e.g. container IP in Docker, or through a reverse proxy) because the HMR WebSocket connection fails. The root cause: `createFromReadableStream` in dev mode waits for **two** streams to complete -- the main RSC data stream and a `debugChannel` stream. The debug channel is fed via HMR WebSocket messages (`REACT_DEBUG_CHUNK`). When the WebSocket fails, the debug channel never closes, so `await initialServerResponse` in `hydrate()` hangs forever, and `createRoot().render()` is never called. ## Reproduction **Environment:** Next.js 16.2.1, React 19.2.3, running inside Docker (Debian) 1. Create an App Router project with `error.tsx` and a server component that throws: ```tsx // src/app/page.tsx (server component) export default async function HomePage() { throw new Error("Database unavailable"); } ``` ```tsx // src/app/error.tsx "use client"; export default function ErrorPage() { return

500 - Server Error

; } ``` 2. Run `next dev` (default: listens on localhost:3000) 3. Access via `localhost:3000` -- error boundary renders correctly ("500") 4. Access via the machine's IP address (e.g. `172.17.0.2:3000` inside Docker) -- **permanently blank page** The browser console on the non-localhost access shows repeated WebSocket failures: ``` WebSocket connection to 'ws://172.17.0.2:3000/_next/webpack-hmr?id=...' failed: Error during WebSocket handshake: net::ERR_INVALID_HTTP_RESPONSE ``` ## Root cause The call chain: 1. SSR fails, Next.js sends an empty HTML shell with `` and inline RSC payload 2. Client-side `hydrate()` runs (in `node_modules/next/dist/client/app-next-turbopack.js`) 3. In dev mode, a `debugChannel` is created from a `TransformStream` and passed to `createFromReadableStream(readable, { debugChannel, ... })` 4. Inside the RSC client runtime (`react-server-dom-turbopack`), `createFromReadableStream` starts reading from **two** streams: ```js // react-server-dom-turbopack/cjs/react-server-dom-turbopack-client.browser.development.js var streamDoneCount = 0, handleDone = function() { 2 === ++streamDoneCount && close(response); }; startReadingFromUniversalStream(response, options.debugChannel.readable, handleDone); startReadingFromStream(response, stream, handleDone, stream); ``` 5. The debug channel's writer is closed via `REACT_DEBUG_CHUNK` messages received over the HMR WebSocket 6. When the WebSocket fails (non-localhost access), no `REACT_DEBUG_CHUNK` messages arrive, the writer is never closed, `streamDoneCount` stays at 1, and `close(response)` is never called 7. `await initialServerResponse` in `hydrate()` never resolves 8. `createRoot().render()` is never called -- permanently blank page ## Proof Patching the Next.js client bundle to pass `debugChannel: undefined` instead of the actual debug channel makes the page render correctly on `172.17.0.2`: ```js // Original: initialServerResponse = createFromReadableStream(readable, { callServer: ..., findSourceMapURL: ..., debugChannel, // <-- blocks when WebSocket fails startTime: 0 }); // Patched: initialServerResponse = createFromReadableStream(readable, { callServer: ..., findSourceMapURL: ..., debugChannel: undefined, // <-- page renders correctly startTime: 0 }); ``` With this patch, the error boundary renders the "500" page on the container IP, even though the WebSocket still fails. ## Impact This affects any dev environment where the browser connects to the Next.js dev server via a non-localhost address: - Docker containers accessed by container IP - Remote development servers - Reverse proxies forwarding to the dev server - VM-based development (e.g. Vagrant, cloud dev environments) The issue only manifests when SSR throws an error (triggering the CSR error boundary path). Normal SSR pages use `hydrateRoot` instead of `createRoot` and may not hit this exact code path. Production builds are unaffected because `debugChannel` is a dev-only feature. ## Suggested fix The debug channel should handle WebSocket failures gracefully. Some options: 1. **Close the debug channel writer when the WebSocket errors/closes** -- in the `REACT_DEBUG_CHUNK` handler area, add cleanup on WebSocket close 2. **Add a timeout** -- if the debug channel receives no data within N seconds, close it 3. **Make the debug channel non-blocking** -- don't require it for the main RSC response to resolve; treat it as best-effort ## Versions - Next.js: 16.2.1 - affected - Next.js: 16.2.0 - affected - Next.js: 16.1.7 - unaffected - React: 19.2.3 - Node.js: 25.8.0 - OS: Debian (Docker container) Your root cause analysis is spot-on. This is an issue introduced with the React 19.2.x debug channel feature. **Workaround (immediate):** Bind the dev server to `0.0.0.0` so the HMR WebSocket URL resolves correctly: ```bash next dev --hostname 0.0.0.0 ``` If you're still hitting WebSocket failures behind a reverse proxy, you can configure the WebSocket URL in `next.config.js`: ```js // next.config.js module.exports = { webSocketUrl: 'auto', }; ``` **Why this happens (confirming your analysis):** The `debugChannel` in `createFromReadableStream` uses a `TransformStream` whose writable side is only closed when `REACT_DEBUG_CHUNK` messages arrive over the HMR WebSocket. The RSC response resolution requires **both** the main stream and the debug channel stream to complete (`streamDoneCount === 2`). When the WebSocket can't connect, the debug channel never closes, and hydration hangs indefinitely. This is specific to the SSR error → CSR fallback path because it uses `createRoot()` instead of `hydrateRoot()`, making it fully dependent on the `initialServerResponse` promise resolving. **The real fix should be upstream** — the debug channel should be non-blocking / best-effort. Your suggested option 3 (don't require it for the main RSC response to resolve) is the cleanest approach. This would likely need a fix in `react-server-dom-turbopack` rather than in Next.js itself. I'd recommend filing this as a **bug report** (not just a discussion) since you have a clear reproduction and it's a regression from 16.1.7 → 16.2.0.

Is it intentional that `/_next/data/` responses in pages router are now all streams?
### Summary

This question comes from this bug: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/90281

That ticket treats this change (which began in 15.4.1) as a bug, but it's entirely possible that this is now expected behavior that should be worked around, if necessary. This change limits our ability to leverage cloudfront for compression _and_ caching, which we would prefer to maintain in our self-hosted setup.

There's a similar discussion from 2022 here (https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/38606) where it appears this is treated as unexpected.

### Additional information

See https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/90281 for code snippets, recreation steps, and all details



### Example

https://github.com/bbrouse/nextjs-content-length-repro
This looks intentional as of 15.4.1. The switch to chunked/streamed responses is part of the RSC pipeline that Next.js now applies across pages and app router.

If you need Content-Length headers for CloudFront caching, you can try setting this in a custom server or middleware.

```js
import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'

export function middleware(request) {
  const response = NextResponse.next()
  if (request.nextUrl.pathname.startsWith('/_next/data')) {
    response.headers.set('Cache-Control', 'public, max-age=3600')
  }
  return response
}
```

Alternatively, you could disable streaming for specific routes using `next.config.js` if you are not using App Router features that require it.

Have you tried setting `experimental.serverActions` or adjusting `output: 'standalone'` in your config? Might help with your self-hosted setup.
This looks like a regression rather than an intentional change - it's not related to the RSC pipeline (that's App Router only).

From what I can tell, the root cause is in `pages-handler.ts`. PR [#80189](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/80189) (merged mid-2025) moved data route handling and wrapped the JSON payload in `Buffer.from()`:

```typescript
new RenderResult(Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(result.value.pageData)), ...)
```

The previous code used `RenderResult.fromStatic(JSON.stringify(...))` which passed a plain string. The problem is that `RenderResult`'s `isDynamic` getter checks `typeof this.response !== 'string'` - a Buffer is an object, not a string, so it returns `true`. That triggers the streaming path in `send-payload.ts`, which skips both the `Content-Length` header and `ETag` generation and pipes the response as chunked instead.

This is the same class of bug that happened in Next.js 12.2.0 (Discussion [#38606](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/38606)) - that one was fixed in v13.2.0.

There's actually already a fix PR open - [#90304](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/90304) - which removes the `Buffer.from()` wrapper. It hasn't been reviewed yet though.

For workarounds until that lands, I'd try one of these (in order of preference):

1. **patch-package** (or `pnpm patch` / `yarn patch`) to apply the same one-line fix from PR #90304 to your installed `next` module. That way you stay on current versions and the fix survives reinstalls.

2. **Pin to 15.4.0** if you haven't picked up anything critical from 15.4.1+. Simplest rollback.

3. **Enable `compress: true`** in next.config.js so Next.js handles compression server-side. CloudFront should then see `Content-Encoding` and pass it through. Adds some CPU load to the origin though.

Adjusting CloudFront config to handle chunked responses is technically possible but pretty fragile - fixing it at the framework level is much cleaner.
https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/90304 has landed - thank you all for bringing this up! It will be in canary soon, make sure to verify it.

Also being backported to 15.5 - https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/91615 keep an eye on that.

Should dashboards default to SSR or stay client-side SPAs?
Building a React dashboard with real-time data (Supabase, analytics, payments). Everyone keeps saying "use Next.js for SSR" but I'm seeing faster dev cycles and simpler deploys with Vite + client-side rendering.
When does SSR actually matter for dashboards? Or is it just cargo-culting best practices from content sites?
Dashboards should stay client-side. SSR is solving the wrong problem.
Here's why:
SSR wins for:

Public content (blogs, marketing, e-commerce)
SEO requirements
First-paint performance for strangers

Dashboards don't need any of that.
Your users are:

Authenticated → They wait for login anyway, SSR's "instant first paint" is irrelevant
Returning daily → Browser caches everything after first visit
Behind auth walls → Zero SEO benefit
Expecting real-time data → You're hydrating from APIs post-render regardless

What actually matters for dashboards:

Fast API responses (optimize your Supabase queries)
Aggressive caching (React Query, SWR with stale-while-revalidate)
Code splitting (lazy load heavy charts/tables)
Optimistic updates (feel fast > be fast)

Vite + React is the right call. Next.js adds:

Serverless complexity
Vendor lock-in (Vercel edge functions)
Extra render cycles (server → hydration → client state)

Ship client-side. Optimize what users actually feel: interactions, not initial paint.

Allow dynamic `serverRuntimeConfig` and `publicRuntimeConfig` values from `process.env.*` with `outputStandalone: true`
### Describe the feature you'd like to request

Currently, using

```json
experimental: {
  outputStandalone: true
}
```

in a `next.config.json` will produce a `server.js` file that will encode the environment variables into the bundle at build-time. 

Currently our `next.config.js` looks like this;

```javascript
module.exports = {
  serverRuntimeConfig: {
    someSecret: process.env.SOME_SECRET,
  },
  publicRuntimeConfig: {
    someValue: process.env.SOME_VALUE,
  }
}
```

and once we have done a `next build` with the standalone experimental bundler, we end up with `server.js` looking something like;

```javascript
// ...
"serverRuntimeConfig": { someSecret: 'test' },
"publicRuntimeConfig": { someValue: '' },
// ...
```

Where it has resolved the `process.env.*` at build-time.

This - although it works - is less than desirable for our use case as we like having control of these variables at runtime when running our Docker image in k8s.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Ideally a way to tell Next.js to _not_ encode/bundle these values at build time, and instead leave them unchanged.

Ideally, I want the `server.js` to remain as;

```javascript
// ...
"serverRuntimeConfig": { someSecret: process.env.SOME_SECRET },
"publicRuntimeConfig": { someValue: process.env.SOME_VALUE },
// ...
```

As this then allows us to inject these `process.env.*` values at runtime, having more control over the application.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

Currently I've experimented with automatically re-writing the `server.js` file once it gets built, and replacing with our pre-defined serverRuntime & publicRuntime config objects. This works perfectly - and is currently running perfectly well in our experimental k8s cluster/deployment pipeline :)

documents.text: How to fix Build Error: Parsing CSS source code failed with turbopack ### Summary At work we are using webpack bundler instead of turbopack but with webpack, having module not found issue with [react-pdf](https://www.npmjs.com/package/react-pdf) when setting workerSrc like below, `pdfjs.GlobalWorkerOptions.workerSrc = new URL('pdfjs-dist/build/pdf.worker.min.mjs', import.meta.url).toString();` > Module not found: ESM packages (pdfjs-dist/build/pdf.worker.min.mjs) need to be imported. Use 'import' to reference the package instead. https://nextjs.org/docs/messages/import-esm-externals. But when switched to turbopack, all works smooth but we currently use [ tui-image-editor@3.15.3](https://www.npmjs.com/package/tui-image-editor) and and tui-color-picker@2.2.8 and have the below imports which triggers parsing CSS source code failed error. ``` import 'tui-image-editor/dist/latest/tui-image-editor.min.css; import 'tui-color-picker/dist/tui-color-picker.min.css; ``` Is there anyway to let turbopack to skip checking the erros and let it import the css as I saw similar [issue](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/66394#issuecomment-2152711600)post where author reported the issue with the css errors to the respective plugin team and closed the issue? I wish there is a way using webpack the below statement works or turbopack is little lenient with css parse errors. `pdfjs.GlobalWorkerOptions.workerSrc = new URL('pdfjs-dist/build/pdf.worker.min.mjs', import.meta.url).toString();` react-pdf author says it is an issue(setting workerSrc) with nextjs not skipping running client side code when using dynamic import with ssr:false. https://github.com/wojtekmaj/react-pdf/issues/2039#issuecomment-3611469611 ### Additional information _No response_ ### Example _No response_ Hey! I ran into something similar — here's what worked for me. ## Webpack + `workerSrc` fix The cleanest fix is using a CDN string instead of `new URL()` — sidesteps the ESM resolution issue entirely: ```js pdfjs.GlobalWorkerOptions.workerSrc = `//unpkg.com/pdfjs-dist@${pdfjs.version}/build/pdf.worker.min.mjs`; ``` If you want to keep it local, just guard it so it only runs client-side: ```js if (typeof window !== 'undefined') { pdfjs.GlobalWorkerOptions.workerSrc = new URL( 'pdfjs-dist/build/pdf.worker.min.mjs', import.meta.url ).toString(); } ``` This works because `new URL()` was firing during SSR where `import.meta.url` doesn't behave the same way. ## Turbopack + `tui-image-editor` CSS errors You can tell Turbopack to skip those problematic CSS files in `next.config.js`: ```js experimental: { turbo: { rules: { '*.css': { loaders: ['ignore-loader'], as: '*.css', }, }, }, }, ``` Not a perfect long-term fix, but it unblocks you while waiting for the plugin maintainers to sort it out on their end. --- The CDN approach for `workerSrc` is honestly the most stable option right now until both libraries fully catch up with their respective bundlers. Hope this helps! Hello chlvbharath. Turbopack is purposefully built on a strict Rust based CSS parser to ensure web specification compliance. Because of this architectural choice it throws hard errors on malformed vendor CSS that Webpack would normally ignore or swallow silently. Unfortunately there is no built in flag in Turbopack to bypass these CSS syntax errors right now. The bundler expects all imported stylesheets to be fully valid. The most reliable workaround for Turbopack is to patch the malformed CSS directly in your node modules using a tool like patch-package or pnpm patch so that the third party library conforms to the standard. Alternatively if you want to stay on Webpack where the CSS parses fine you can fix your react-pdf module issue by taking the web worker script and copying it into your public directory. Then you can point the workerSrc to the absolute public path rather than relying on the bundler to resolve the ESM import URL dynamically. What [tui-image-editor](https://www.npmjs.com/package/tui-image-editor) version do you have? Feels like they might have fixed this issue?

Why is my React useEffect Hook running twice on page load?
### Summary

I am building a Next.js / React application, and I have a useEffect hook that fetches data from an API when the component mounts using the empty dependency array [].

However, when I look at my console logs, I can see that the fetch request is firing two times instead of just once whenever I load the page.

Is this a bug in React, or am I doing something wrong with my hook?

### Additional information

_No response_

### Example

_No response_
This is actually the intended behavior in React 18 when you are in development mode!

React automatically wraps your application in <React.StrictMode>. In development, Strict Mode unmounts and remounts every component automatically whenever it is rendered for the first time. This is done on purpose to help you find bugs related to side effects and to ensure your useEffect cleanup functions are working properly.

How to handle it:

Option 1 (Recommended): Add a cleanup function Make sure your effect cleans up after itself (e.g., aborting a fetch request):

javascript
useEffect(() => {
  const controller = new AbortController();
  
  fetch('/api/data', { signal: controller.signal })
    .then(res => res.json())
    .then(data => console.log(data));
    
  return () => controller.abort(); // Cleanup
}, []);
Option 2: Disable Strict Mode (Not Recommended) If you are using Next.js and really want to turn this off, you can open next.config.js and set reactStrictMode: false.

Note: The double execution only happens in development. When you build and deploy to production, the useEffect will only run once!

Proposal: Integrate server-only as a first-class utility in next core
### Goals

**Zero-Config Security**: Eliminate the requirement to manually install server-only as a separate peer dependency for every project.

**Improved Discoverability**: Make server-side enforcement part of the standard next API (e.g., next/server-only), making it easier for new developers to find.

**Package Consistency**: Reduce the "fragmentation" of having to manage a tiny, single-purpose external package for a core Next.js architectural concept.

### Non-Goals

_No response_

### Background

Currently, the `server-only` [package](https://www.npmjs.com/package/server-only) is a fundamental part of the Next.js security story. It ensures that sensitive code—such as database queries or internal business logic—never accidentally leaks into Client Components.

While the [documentation](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/data-security#preventing-client-side-execution-of-server-only-code) recommends it, it currently exists as a separate dependency that developers must remember to npm install.

### Proposal

I propose that Next.js should export a built-in `server-only` marker directly from the next package. This would streamline the setup process and ensure that security best practices are baked directly into the framework.
- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/server-and-client-components#preventing-environment-poisoning

> In Next.js, installing server-only or client-only is optional. However, if your linting rules flag extraneous dependencies, you may install them to avoid issues.
>
> Next.js handles server-only and client-only imports internally to provide clearer error messages when a module is used in the wrong environment. The contents of these packages from NPM are not used by Next.js.

It is already automatically interpreted by the framework. Next.js does some additional checks to make sure you get better errors when a module ends up in the wrong module graph.

Better support for runtime environment variables.
### Describe the feature you'd like to request

When dealing with Docker based deployments on different environments, it's very useful to be able to specify environment variables for thinks like the base url for api calls, or a token for a analytics service.

Currently, it seems that next.js only properly supports specifying environment variables at build time, this leads to the following issue when using Docker.

1. Build the docker image on CI with a specific (environment) configuration.
2. Push the docker image to a repository.
3. Pull/start the docker image on testing/staging/acceptance/production.
4. Changing environment variables have no effect.

### Describe the solution you'd like

I think there are type of environment variable that need to able to override:

 - Frontend specific configuration (tokens for services like analytics).
 - Backend/forntend configuration required for server side rendering the work correctly (api base url).

Being able to override the environment variables runtime would solve the first problem, but additional work on the server side render is probably also needed to support these cases properly.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

An alternative would be to build specific Docker images for specific environments, however. I think this is considered an anti-pattern and should preferably be avoided.
To continue this discussion here: I full agree to the input/request from @svenvandescheur . We're deploying our application to different environments which have a variety of different configurations (endpoints, tokes etc.). 

The solution right now results in building many identical images in the pipeline with different build args. 

One build runs 15min including the upload to the registry. With every environment we're adding, we add 15min build time (or resources if run in parallel). This is a mess. 

For other client side only projects the solution is straight forward. We're using an nginx proxy with `sub_filter` to replace the relevant variables. But this won't work here since the server side executed code has substituted variables too.    
Another post in agreement - I'm new to Next.js and was surprised to find it does not support runtime environment variables, as they're a common best-practice pattern for building modern 12 factor apps and/or those deployed via Docker. A big selling point of using Docker to begin with is to be able to build one image and have it work everywhere - dev, test, staging, production, etc - and having to "bake" in environment-specific configuration at build-time is antithetical to that goal. 

Speaking of my specific deployment process for a backend service as an example of what I'd expect, I use AWS secrets manager to store and manage access to various environment configurations which then get injected into the docker environment at runtime using ECS + Fargate (though this could be any orchestrator). Doing it this way both lets me easily set up any number of arbitrary environments/configurations and control access to sensitive configuration info (e.g. API keys, database credentials, etc), only allowing a given container instance access to the config it needs to run and restricting access everywhere else. Versus if it is baked into the image, anyone who has access to pull that image also has access to that "baked in" information (and rotation of secrets always requires a rebuild of the image), and in order to build the image, there needs to be a build machine that has access to that configuration info (realistically probably for all environments unless you have a separate build machine for every environment) so that it can generate a .env file for a given environment. Additionally I also can't build a "production" image on my local machine (say I'm troubleshooting something or the build machine goes down) without placing production credentials on my local machine. So now I have potentially sensitive info in a few places (the image, the build machine, a local machine) that needs to be managed. Build-time variables make sense when they're not sensitive and don't vary by environment, but are really problematic and clumsy for anything else.

As I said, I am new to Next, so if there's just some functionality I missed or I misunderstood the environment variable docs, I'd love to hear about it. Otherwise has anyone come up with a solution that doesn't involve creating multiple image variants when the server-side env varies?
