documents.text: Confusion Around Next.js Component for LCP / Above-the-Fold Images ### Summary I’m a bit confused about how to properly configure the Next.js `` component when the image is **above the fold** and also the **LCP (Largest Contentful Paint)** element. ## Current Understanding (Plain HTML) In standard HTML, for an LCP image, we would typically do something like: ```html ``` This makes sense because: - `loading="eager"` → ensures the image is not lazy-loaded - `fetchpriority="high"` → signals to the browser that this resource is important (LCP candidate) This setup is straightforward and aligns with performance best practices. --- ## The Confusion in Next.js According to the Next.js documentation for the `` component: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/components/image#preload > When not to use it: > - When the `loading` property is used. > - When the `fetchPriority` property is used. It mentions **not to use `preload` together with `loading`**. So which configuration is correct for an above-the-fold LCP image in Next.js? ### Option 1 ```tsx ``` ### Option 2 ```tsx ``` That makes me unsure about the correct way to configure an above-the-fold LCP image in Next.js. Would really appreciate clarification on the intended pattern for LCP images so I can avoid misconfiguration and follow the framework’s performance guidance correctly. ### Additional information _No response_ ### Example _No response_ This is a lovely topic... So `preload` is more about starting to download an asset, before it is actually discovered. If your LCP, over the fold image, is the buried under tons of CSS links, JS scripts, and other HTML, it won't be discovered and queued for download until the browser gets to that part of the HTML. `loading` is more about, after discovery, should the browser download it eagerly, or is it ok to wait, as a function of the distance to the viewport. Note that, even if in the viewport, a `lazy` loaded image, gets deprioritized in favor of other assets, which is why you definitely don't want to lazy load an LCP candidate, above the fold etc. - there's a level of uncertainty that you opt-in to with lazy loaded images, which is why it is better to be explicitly eager! `fetchPriority` is more like, ok, we have discovered the image, and are about to download it, but there's other assets being downloaded, let's hint to the browser that our asset should be pushed forward in the queue. When you `preload` an asset, it is queued to be downloaded when the browser discovers its `link` in the head of the document, likely before anything else. The `img` tag that renders the image, might not even be in the document yet as the HTML chunks arrive. Whereas, `loading` is, after discovery, as a function of distance to the viewport, download it. Since next/image defaults to lazy loading, you have to make it explicitly eager, and because the asset was just discovered, you give it high fetch priority. As with most things in webdev, here you have to make a choice. For a single, clear LCP hero image, using preload is a good default. For many other cases, eager loading with high priority may be the better fit. When you say in plain HTML, I'd do this, you are considering only the case where discoverability of the image asset is not a problem. - https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Attributes/rel/preload There’s a lot of nuance here, but the key distinction is whether you’re solving late discovery or network prioritization. However, when I switch to using only `preload`, I receive a warning related to image fetch priority. Due to this restriction in Next.js — where `preload` cannot be used alongside `loading` and `fetchPriority` — I’m unable to fully satisfy Lighthouse recommendations for optimizing the LCP image. Confusion Regarding <script> for JSON-LD Schema
In the [documentation](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/json-ld), it says:
> Our current recommendation for JSON-LD is to render structured data as a `<script>` tag in your layout.js or page.js components.

Is this a typo, or are we supposed to use the native `<script>` tag instead of the `<Script>` from `next/script` when rendering JSON-LD?

The `next/script` element is for JavaScript. The `JSON-LD` convention is to put it in a script tag with a non JavaScript content type. Which is why a `next/script` doesn't really apply. It might work, but it is not what that Script tag is for.

In other words, `JSON-LD` is not executable JavaScript.

`script` tags are used by the industry/standard/specs to carry all sorts of mime types, like JSON, importmaps, speculation rules too IIRC, arguably none of those concerns the `next/script` tag.

We've set the revalidation time with next.revalidate as part of Apollo fetchOptions to 24 hours.

Yet I am seeing **cache MISS** logs in Vercel for these queries multiple times an hour.

**This is a much higher rate than expected**. The hit rate in Vercel Observability is only 50%, we would expect 90%+. This increases backend load and our Vercel usage costs.

What could explain this? Why is the cache not honoring the revalidation rate? LRU limits? Something else?

### Additional information

```js
Some info on our app:

- Next 16, Turbopack, NOT cacheComponents (we tried but hit too many bugs), App Router (for pages where we see this behavior), deployed on Vercel.
- We have some marketing pages, but most of our app is a purchase funnel for a product among 20k+ products, identified by a slug. These pages a dynamic due to usage of cookies, searchParams, etc.
- I am seeing the non-honored cache behavior on the product detail page query in particular. It returns slow-changing data, hence why we want to cache it for 24h in order to avoid unnecessary load and compute. We are expecting one cache entry per product slug, so about 20k, which seems reasonable?
```

documents.text:
How to Preserve SSG Cached Pages After Redeployment on Vercel?
I am using `Vercel`, and I have many fully static (SSG) pages. Whenever I redeploy the application, Whenever I redeploy the application, SSG pages are built again.

I understand that rebuilding everything has benefits, especially when there are UI or code changes. However, since I have a large number of SSG pages, I would prefer not to rebuild all of them on every redeployment.

Is there any way to preserve or retain those cached SSG pages on Vercel even after redeployment?
I ran into the same limitation when scaling a large SSG project on Vercel. The short answer is that on Vercel every deployment is immutable. A new deployment creates a completely new build artifact. That means all SSG pages are regenerated during the build step. There is no native way to “reuse” the HTML files from a previous deployment.

Vercel does not persist `.next` build output between deployments. The cache they provide only speeds up dependency installation and build tooling, not pre rendered pages.

If you want to avoid rebuilding everything, the practical approaches are architectural:

One option is to switch from pure SSG to ISR. With Incremental Static Regeneration, pages are generated on demand and cached at the edge. After a redeploy, pages are regenerated only when requested instead of all at build time. This is usually the cleanest solution.

Another approach is reducing `getStaticPaths` size and using fallback modes so not every page is prebuilt.

If your content rarely changes, you could also move heavy static content outside the Next.js build process and host it separately, for example in object storage or a CDN.

But strictly speaking, there is no setting in Vercel that preserves previously generated SSG pages across deployments. A redeploy always means a fresh build.

The thing is, AFAIK, there’s no reliable mechanism to know which ISR pages are affected (or not) by a new build. The rendering output depends on code, data fetching, and runtime behavior, so each deployment is isolated.

Since each deployment has its own ISR cache. That makes things predictable and safe: new code won’t accidentally reuse HTML generated by older logic, and rollbacks work instantly because they restore the previous deployment + cache together.

If you want persistence across deployments, that’s what the Data Cache (`fetch` caching) is for, it lives outside the deployment boundary. With Cache Components, the `remote` directive can also use Data Cache IIRC, but right now the `buildId` is part of the cache key.

In general, it’s better to separate “content changes” from “code changes,” so content updates don’t force ISR regeneration tied to deployments. And remember there’s still a CDN layer in front smoothing things out.

documents.text:
Does `use cache` make the build non-deterministic?
### Summary

Normally, I would expect my build to be deterministic, meaning if it succeeds the first time, it will always succeed especially across multiple deployments.
However, if you have a function that needs network request to external API or even your own backend, and you use `use cache` to include it in the pre-rendered static shell. Then, `next build` can potentially fail if the API is down, in a sense, your build success now is contingent/dependent upon external factor. In other words, my deployment can succeed today but the same deployment can fail sometime later.
Am I understanding it correctly or missing something?

### Additional information

_No response_

### Example

_No response_
The reason why certain operations, dynamic data access or Math.random, etc, suspend by default (require a fallback) is exactly what you describe. They are all truly asynchronous work, (in this context not limited to JS async mechanics necessarily), they take an indeterminate time to complete, under which we consider them pending, and might resolve or reject, and/or yield different results every time you call them.

What `use cache` allows you to do at build time, is to take a snapshot in time of these operations at-the-time-of-build, by actually running them, and paying upfront the time cost, and storing that result into the static shell (even Math.random). Further more you assign a cacheLife (explicitly or implicitly) stating for how long this is an acceptable snapshot of the data. 

The key thing here is, whether an operation at build time rejects or not, and if that changes the inherent deterministic nature of the your applications build step, is not given by `use cache` - the directive is not what makes builds non-deterministic - that's just what working with asynchronous operations has in store for you.

> If you need builds to be “always green” even when dependencies are flaky: don’t make the build depend on those dependencies. Defer to request time with <Suspense> and/or render a fallback/error state.
> 
> If you’re okay with “snapshot what we can at prerender time”: use use cache, set an appropriate cacheLife, and code defensively (try/catch or error boundaries) so an outage doesn’t automatically become a failed build.

With `use cache` though you can do interesting things like (and though you could also with ISR, that still made you opt-in the entire route into static, whereas Cache Components lets you have static and dynamic parts):

If you build today with a cache life of `"hours"` assigned to some data, and then wait a few hours to start the server, then upon start, you'll see stale data (`"hours"` expires after 1 day, but does stale-while-revalidate after 1 hour) - and the shell will be patched. 

If the process that generates this data fails, you can still assign a shorter cache life to that (**but not too short**).

If your API service is down, then you might choose to act on that in the code, and render a different branch, under `use cache` still, that renders a message: `API is down - we're looking into it`.

Then it really depends on the business case, if your service is truly down, then eventually all users, regardless of deployment instance, will start to see the error message, and depending on your revalidate/expire timings, the server will try to regenerate this UI, hopefully without overloading a fallen service.

documents.text:
Unexpected high serverless function usage on Vercel with Next.js App Router
Hi everyone 👋

I’m running a Next.js (App Router) project on Vercel and noticed that my **Serverless Function usage is much higher than expected**, even though most of my pages should be cached.

I’m trying to understand what might be causing this.

### Setup

* Next.js App Router
* Deployed on Vercel
* Using `fetch` with `revalidate`
* No obvious API routes being hit frequently
* Traffic is moderate, but function invocations are surprisingly high

### What confuses me

I assumed that after the first request, pages would be served from cache and wouldn’t keep invoking serverless functions.

But Vercel analytics show functions running far more often than expected.

### Questions

* What patterns in App Router cause functions to run on every request?
* Does using cookies, headers, or dynamic data force SSR every time?
* How can I verify whether a route is truly cached vs dynamically rendered?
* What’s the best way to reduce unnecessary function executions?

If anyone has insights into this or debugging tips, I’d really appreciate the help.

Thanks!

Hi! This is a very common confusion with the App Router on Vercel.

What usually happens is that something in the route is silently forcing it to be **dynamic**, so Vercel can’t serve it from the cache and has to run the Serverless Function on every request.

The most common triggers are:

* Using `cookies()` or `headers()` anywhere in the tree
* Reading request-specific data
* `fetch` without proper caching config
* Setting `cache: 'no-store'`
* Using Server Actions in the same route
* Having `export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'` (even indirectly)

Any of these make the route **SSR on every hit**.

### How to verify

Check the response headers in the browser:

* If you see: `x-vercel-cache: HIT` → served from cache
* If you see: `MISS` or `BYPASS` → function executed

### How to fix

Make sure your data fetching looks like this:

```ts
await fetch(url, {
  next: { revalidate: 60 },
});
```

Avoid using `cookies()` / `headers()` in pages that should be cached. If you need them, move that logic to a separate dynamic route or API route.

You can also explicitly force static behavior:

```ts
export const dynamic = 'force-static';
```

Once the route becomes truly static/ISR, you’ll see function usage drop and `x-vercel-cache` start returning `HIT`.

Hope this saves you some function invocations 
- What patterns in App Router cause functions to run on every request?

Without Cache Components on, pages are either, fully static, or fully dynamic. There isn't really a good in-between hybrid. A fully dynamic page gets to access latest data and such, but needs to be mindful of Suspense states to start pushing out UI to the browser as it renders to completion.

A fully static page serves from CDN, immediately, but might have stale data. To try and marry these two ideas, ISR was introduced, a static page that regenerates itself, at runtime, given certain parameters.

The key bit here is that fully dynamic page in the current model, is any page that access so-called dynamic data within its React tree. 

Dynamic data in this model are things such as cookies, searchParams, headers, etc - these are only known when a request arrives, so they can't be statically prerendered. There's also fetch, and the part that's a bit confusing in the current model, not-in-cache-components, that you can make fetch explicitly cached, or mark it as data that may be stale for a revalidate time, and that changes how the page behaves.

- Does using cookies, headers, or dynamic data force SSR every time?

Yes. In Cache Components this nuanced and likely more close to what you'd expect.

- How can I verify whether a route is truly cached vs dynamically rendered?

The build output prints clearly which routes are fully static, dynamic, and such, each route gets an icon and the icon legend is printed at the bottom.

- What’s the best way to reduce unnecessary function executions?

Depends on your use case. If you want to show financial info by the second, you are likely going to need to more frequent server function execution. If you are showing the list of the first 150 pokemon, you can statically render that on a page and that and cut your runtime server function execution to zero.

updateTag vs revalidateTag
Don't understand real difference of these both?
revalidateTag mark invalidate data cache entries for given tag and fully rerenders current route in browser.
updateTag mark invalidate data cache entries for given tag, refetch invalidated data for current route in browser and rerender full route.
So what is real difference, since in all case currrent route fully rerenders, so invalidated by tag data with both case refreshes while renders?
For invalidated data in other routes both only mark them as invalid.
Thanks in advance!
`revalidateTag` is now, more in line with stale-while-revalidate, meaning that stale data is served, while it is revalidated in the "background".

`updateTag` is more of a `read-your-write` handler. It'll mark the data as expired, forcing any new data fetches to block until the data resolves. 

- https://nextjs.org/docs/beta/app/api-reference/functions/updateTag#differences-from-revalidatetag

I should mention that documentation is often far from ideal. Especially now, when we have many changes in behavior.
Of course, I read this, but I didn't found any difference in practice, but I will check again.
Next question - we have now two different caching API - 1)fetch on pair with unstable_cache
2)'use cache'
are revalidateTag and updateTag have equal behavior for both strategies or new behavior only for new 'use cache'?
And why do we have updateTag but not updatePath with similar changes compare to revalidatePath?
Both revalidateTag() and updateTag() invalidate cache entries for the given tag, but the key difference is when the data refetch happens.

revalidateTag(tag) only marks the data as stale — the refetch and rerender happen on the next navigation or refresh.

updateTag(tag) immediately triggers a client-side refetch of all data using that tag and rerenders the current route right away.

So:

revalidateTag = “invalidate now, update later.”

updateTag = “invalidate and update now.”

Support a pattern like `Vary` for ISR (opt-out of dynamic rendering)
From the [data fetching caching docs](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/building-your-application/data-fetching/fetching-caching-and-revalidating):

> Next.js provides helpful functions you may need when fetching data in Server Components such as [cookies](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cookies) and [headers](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/functions/headers). These will cause the route to be dynamically rendered as they rely on request time information.

Over time, I ran into some cases where a route opts into dynamic rendering, disabling the `cache-control` response header.

**Examples:**

1. A proxy passes an `x-auth` authorization header to the app, which should be forwarded to API calls. This is different from a user-specific authorization header in that it is required for non-user-specific endpoints too. I understand that an environment parameter could be used in a similar way, this is mostly about being able to integrate with existing infrastructure.
2. A proxy generates an `x-request-id` header that is passed to the app and needs to be forwarded to all API calls. In this case, the API calls might reach through multiple levels between services and the ID is important to group relevant logs.

As soon as `headers().get(…)` is called, Next.js disables [the full route cache](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/building-your-application/caching#full-route-cache).

HTTP supports [the Vary header](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Vary) to describe the headers that influence the response.

I'm wondering if something like this could be supported by Next.js too.

**Example:**

```tsx
// page.tsx

// Only if these headers are read via `headers().get(…)`, 
// then the full route cache is skipped. Additionally, some
// headers like `host` can still support CDN caching in
// case the header is part of the cache key.
export const vary = ['authorization'];
```

Alternatively, there could also be a list of explicitly allowed headers that don't influence the response.

See also: [Understanding The Vary Header](https://www.smashingmagazine.com/2017/11/understanding-vary-header/)

It's now possible to customize `cache-control` as of v14.2.10. Please upgrade and give it a try!

https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/69802
My use case was for a self-hosted setup, I was able to implement this with a custom server: https://github.com/amannn/nextjs-request-store/commit/e6881f33e8d6aa568baeabed7467864976e0ca64

How to properly implement use cache with Next.js 16 App Router — replacing old implicit caching? Hi everyone 👋 I recently upgraded from Next.js 15 to Next.js 16 and I'm trying to migrate from the old implicit caching behavior to the new explicit use cache directive. My app uses the App Router with several dynamic routes that fetch data from an external API. Previously, Next.js handled caching implicitly via fetch() options, but this often led to confusing and unpredictable cache behavior. Now with use cache, I have a few questions: What's the recommended pattern for using use cache alongside Server Components that fetch from external APIs? Should I place it at the layout level, page level, or individual component level? How does use cache interact with Partial Prerendering (PPR)? Can I combine both effectively for routes that have a mix of static and dynamic content? For pages that need revalidation every few minutes, is use cache with a revalidation time the right approach, or should I still use ISR? Has anyone run into issues with Turbopack builds and use cache in production? Any examples or migration tips would be really appreciated! Environment: Next.js 16.1, React 19, Node.js 22, Turbopack, deployed on self-hosted (not Vercel) **1. Where to place `use cache`:** Place it as close to the data fetching as possible — ideally at the **individual component or function level**, not the layout. This gives you granular control. Example: ```tsx async function ProductList() { 'use cache' cacheLife('hours') const data = await fetch('https://api.example.com/products') return } ``` You *can* add it at the page or layout level, but that caches everything — which is rarely what you want with external APIs. **2. `use cache` + PPR:** They work great together. PPR splits your page into a static shell and dynamic parts. Use `use cache` on the cacheable parts, and wrap truly dynamic parts (user-specific data) in ``. The cached components become part of the static shell automatically. ```tsx export default async function Page() { return (
{/* use cache inside */} Loading...

}> {/* runs at request time */}
) } ``` **3. Revalidation every few minutes:** Use `use cache` with `cacheLife` — this replaces ISR for App Router: ```tsx import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache' async function getData() { 'use cache' cacheLife({ stale: 60, revalidate: 300, expire: 3600 }) return fetch('https://api.example.com/data').then(r => r.json()) } ``` ISR still works but `use cache` + `cacheLife` is the recommended approach going forward. **4. Turbopack + `use cache` in production:** Turbopack builds are stable in Next.js 16. No known issues specifically with `use cache`. Just make sure you enable it in config: ```ts // next.config.ts const nextConfig = { cacheComponents: true, } ``` For self-hosted deployments, note that `use cache` uses **in-memory caching** by default. If you're running multiple instances, consider `use cache: remote` with a custom cache handler to share cache across replicas — otherwise each instance maintains its own cache.

I ran `yarn build`, and then `yarn start`, I went to the browser, and `window.next` has the 14.2.5 version.

```shell

```

Then used I the code above, and `yarn start` again, without building, and went to the browser, cleared my cache, and reloaded the page, and now `window.next` shows `xx.xx.xx` :) 

It might not be enough though, maybe Wappalyzer check the files names `_next`, or other heuristics. 
Thanks to @ivanafanasyeu’s solution I was able to remove the Next.js version successfully.  
However, a few files still contained the version string. I updated the script to handle those cases and made it more dynamic so it works reliably in GitLab pipelines and Docker builds.

### Improvements I made
- **Dynamically detects the installed Next.js version** from `node_modules/next/package.json`, ensuring it matches the version actually used in the build.  
- **Cleans all `.next` artifacts** (`.next/static`, `.next/server/chunks`, `.next/diagnostics`, etc.) where the version might appear.  
- **Idempotent and safe**: does not fail if the version is already stripped or not found.  
- **Pipeline- and Docker-friendly**: runs reliably in CI/CD environments without manual intervention.  
- **Provides clear logs** showing which version was removed and how many files were affected.  

### Final solution
1. Create a `scripts/strip-next-version.sh` file at the project root:

```bash
#!/bin/sh
set -e

echo "[postbuild] Stripping Next.js version from .next artifacts for security…"

# Get the actual installed Next.js version
NEXT_VERSION=$(node -p "require('./node_modules/next/package.json').version" 2>/dev/null || echo "")

if [ -z "$NEXT_VERSION" ]; then
  echo "[postbuild] ⚠️ Could not detect Next.js version. Skipping strip step."
  exit 0
fi

# Find all files containing the version
FILES=$(grep -rlF "$NEXT_VERSION" .next || true)

if [ -z "$FILES" ]; then
  echo "[postbuild] ✅ No occurrences of $NEXT_VERSION found in .next."
  exit 0
fi

# Replace version with empty string
echo "$FILES" | xargs sed -i "s/$NEXT_VERSION//g"

echo "[postbuild] ✅ Removed Next.js version $NEXT_VERSION from $(echo "$FILES" | wc -l) files."
```

2. Make the script executable:
```bash
chmod +x scripts/strip-next-version.sh
```

3. Add the script as a postbuild command in `package.json`. This way it runs automatically after build command:
```json
"scripts": {
  "build": "next build --turbopack",
  "postbuild": "./scripts/strip-next-version.sh",
},
```

If everything works correctly, you’ll see output like this after the build:
```
○  (Static)   prerendered as static content
ƒ  (Dynamic)  server-rendered on demand


> my-app@1.0.0 postbuild
> ./scripts/strip-next-version.sh

[postbuild] Stripping Next.js version from .next artifacts for security…
[postbuild] ✅ Removed Next.js version 15.5.2 from 42 files.
```

**Note 1:** If your team works on different OSs (especially Windows) you may need to handle executable permission more gracefully. Like this:
```bash
git add --chmod=+x scripts/strip-next-version.sh
```

**Note 2:** These commands and scripts are written for the Bash shell, if you use other shells you may need to update accordingly. I personally use the Fish shell and haven’t encountered any issues.

Why are react and react-dom versions required in package.json when App Router handles them internally?
According to the Next.js documentation on React version handling:

The `react`/`react-dom` in your package.json serves as a contract for external tooling (TypeScript, testing, linting, IDE) rather than the actual React used at runtime.

) } ``` ### `/app/dashboard/@navbar/kanban/page.tsx` ```tsx export default function KanbanNavbar() { return <>Kanban Navbar } ``` ### `/app/dashboard/@navbar/default.tsx` ```tsx export default function Default() { return <>Default Navbar } ``` ### `/app/dashboard/@navbar/layout.tsx` ```tsx export default function Layout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) { return ( <>

@navbar layout start

{children}

@navbar layout end

) } ``` Now, in the browser if I go this route it renders properly, `/dashboard/kanban` But if I delete `/app/dashboard/@navbar/kanban/*` Now it renders only the default.tsx without the layout Isn't it supposed to render like the following? # Workaround Deleting `/app/dashboard/@navbar/default.tsx` and adding `/app/dashboard/@navbar/[...default]/page.tsx` works! This is actually **expected behavior** in Next.js Parallel Routes. Here's why: ## How `default.tsx` Works in Parallel Routes When Next.js can't find a matching slot for a parallel route (like when you navigate to `/dashboard/kanban` but there's no `@navbar/kanban` directory), it falls back to `default.tsx`. However, `default.tsx` is treated as a **direct replacement for the slot content**, not as a page that goes through the slot's layout. ### The Behavior: 1. **With `/app/dashboard/@navbar/kanban/page.tsx` present:** - Renders: `@navbar/layout.tsx` → `@navbar/kanban/page.tsx` - Layout wrapper is applied ✅ 2. **Without the kanban directory (using `default.tsx`):** - Renders: `@navbar/default.tsx` directly - Layout wrapper is **NOT** applied ⚠️ ## Why This Happens `default.tsx` is designed to be a **fallback slot content**, not a page in the routing system. It's rendered directly into the slot without going through the segment's layout hierarchy. ## Solutions ### Option 1: Include Layout in `default.tsx` (Recommended) Wrap your default content with the layout explicitly: ```tsx // /app/dashboard/@navbar/default.tsx import NavbarLayout from './layout'; export default function Default() { return ( <>Default Navbar ) } ``` ### Option 2: Use Catch-all Route (Your Workaround) Your workaround using `[...default]/page.tsx` works because it's treated as an actual route segment, which does go through the layout: ```tsx // /app/dashboard/@navbar/[...default]/page.tsx export default function CatchAll() { return <>Default Navbar } ``` This makes it a proper page route, so the layout applies. ### Option 3: Move Layout Logic to Parent If the layout styling needs to be consistent, apply it at the parent layout level: ```tsx // /app/dashboard/layout.tsx export default function Layout(props: LayoutProps<'/dashboard'>) { return (
{props.navbar}
{props.children}
) } ``` ## Recommendation For your use case, **Option 2** (catch-all route) is cleanest since it maintains the routing hierarchy properly and allows the slot's layout to work as expected for all routes. ## Reference This behavior is documented in the [Next.js Parallel Routes documentation](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/building-your-application/routing/parallel-routes#defaultjs) under the `default.js` section.

For the first request to be blocking is acceptable, but for the request after the revalidate period (before expire) it is expected that the cached data is returned instead of revalidating the cached data synchronously. I am not sure if this is the expected behavior, from the docs page: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife#revalidate it does not seem like it should be synchronously revalidating.

Hey, this is a known issue with `"use cache"` in dynamic routes. You're not alone - several people have run into this exact behavior.

The core problem is that when a `"use cache"` function runs at runtime (in a dynamic context), Next.js treats the cached data as "expired" rather than "stale" after the revalidate period. This means it blocks and regenerates synchronously instead of serving stale content while revalidating in the background.

There's an open issue tracking this: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/74882 - it describes the exact same behavior where dynamic routes don't get stale-while-revalidate semantics that static routes get.

A few things that might help as workarounds:

1. **Use `generateStaticParams`** with at least one entry (even if you don't want to pre-render everything). This signals to Next.js that the route should use ISR behavior. Other paths not in the array will still be generated on-demand but should then cache properly.

2. **Avoid wrapping the cached component with Suspense** (including `loading.tsx`) - there seems to be some interaction between suspense boundaries and the caching behavior that causes issues.

3. If your use case allows, **move the expensive work to a separate cached function** that doesn't depend on dynamic params, then compose it with the dynamic data.

Unfortunately there's no perfect solution right now. The expectation (and docs) suggest it should work the way you expect - stale data served while revalidating - but it doesn't in dynamic contexts. This seems to be on the team's radar though.

Hope this helps clarify what's going on!

What is a technical definition of "hydration" within NextJS?
The terms _hydration_, _rehydration_, _hydrate_, etc. appear periodically in NextJS documentation, but I'm unclear exactly what they refer to.

[For example](https://nextjs.org/docs/advanced-features/automatic-static-optimization):

> Statically generated pages are still reactive: Next.js will hydrate your application client-side to give it full interactivity.

From context clues (and ReactJS [documentation](https://reactjs.org/docs/react-dom.html#hydrate)) it seems hydration is the process of imbuing server-rendered HTML with the client-side JS necessary for dynamic elements or interaction? But I would appreciate a more technical definition. Is hydration a specific _event_? A general concept accomplished in many ways? A specific function or method? Is it just inherited from ReactJS with no changes?

Thanks dearly!
I'm trying to figure this out too. I'm honestly not sure if this is correct, so I would appreciate clarifications and corrections. I'm trying to compare this to concepts like reconciliation and First Contentful Paint.

`hydration`: This is the process of attaching react listeners to already-existing html dom nodes.

`rehydration`: This is pretty much the same thing, but is used in reference to SSR - SSR returns full html, but you still need to attach the react listeners to it. 

`Next.js-before-hydration`: this is the stage starting from the request to the server, through loading the html content in the browser to the point that the (re)-hydration process can begin. Depending on how your site is structured, this stage can end before or after the FCP is registered.

`Next.js-hydration`: See hydration above. This can end before or after FCP is registered, but I think it always ends before the onLoad timing event. 

What's left is react reconciliation - I think that if that single page loads leads to a lot of additional commits, there's a reconciliation process that happens after the end of `Next.js-hydration`.

I'm not sure how this relates to the number of commits in React Profiler for a single page load. I *think* that all commits after first commit will happen after `Next.js-hydration` begins. 

A __hydration__ means "Each generated HTML is associated with minimal JavaScript code necessary for that page. When a page is loaded by the browser, its JavaScript code runs and makes the page fully interactive "

TypeScript Error: Cannot Find Module for Global CSS Imports
### Summary

Has anyone else encountered this issue? This wasn’t happening before, but now I’m getting a TypeScript error across the entire project on the global CSS imports:

**“Cannot find module or type declarations for side-effect import of '@styles/globals.css'. ts(2882)”**

Any ideas on what might be causing this and how to fix it?

### Additional information

_No response_

### Example

_No response_
Hi @Adithmd04!
This usually happens if your `moduleResolution` in `tsconfig.json` is set to `nodenext` / `node16` but TypeScript can't find the type definitions for css files.
**The Fix:**
Create a file named `declarations.d.ts` (or add to your existing `env.d.ts`) in your root/src folder:
```ts
declare module '*.css';
```
Alternatively, ensure your next-env.d.ts is actually generated and included in your tsconfig.json "include" array! Next.js usually handles this automatically, but sometimes it gets excluded.

How to pass fetched data to client components without streaming when cacheComponents is enabled? ### Summary Hello. I'm fetching and caching data in a function using the "use cache" directive. I'm calling and awaiting the function in a server component, but when I want to pass the fetched data to a client component, it wants me to wrap the client component in a Suspense tag, but I don't want to stream the fetched data; I want it to be prerendered and be interactive at the client side. ### Additional information _No response_ ### Example _No response_ Hi @AmirHosseinNP `` does not automatically mean streaming. Suspense is just the mechanism React uses when something can suspend. If your page is pre-rendered (SSG) or server-rendered without streaming, Suspense can still be present and your output can still be fully prerendered HTML. Make sure you pass plain serializable data (no Promises, no class instances, no Dates without conversion, no BigInt, no Response objects). {JSON.stringify(data, null, 2)}
; } ``` If Next still asks for Suspense, it’s a signal that `data` isn’t actually a `plain resolved value` in a way it can serialize safely. normalize it: ```js const json = await res.json(); return JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(json)); // brute-force normalization ```

documents.text:
Using NextJS to server-render standalone HTML for embedding in a page
### Summary

Is there an approach to inlining the result of a Next.js server-rendered page inside another page (e.g. as a microfrontend).

From initial experiments, attempting to use a Next.js page as an island microfrontend breaks the 'hosting' page. Next makes the strong assumption that it owns the document body, and doesn't consider itself 'mounted' at some particular root node. If you inline a Next page inside another page, it therefore proceeds to label the whole page body as an inconsistent hydration. This causes removal of all pre-existing content as soon as the Next.js javascript bundle is initialised.

Is there some way to determine an explicit React root node binding that allows NextJS to look after only its own part of the page  - any configuration options to assist with this?

With NextJS constrained to operate within some uniquely identified root node on the page, (avoiding hydration inconsistencies or 'taking over' the page), this should allow sibling elements to be left alone that 'belong' to some other framework even though NextJs could find them under the same HTML document body.

We have previously used Vite to create standalone HTML which can be directly inlined in another HTML page,  with Vite practices seeming to align with this approach out of the box (via an explicit root node definition). Delivering this with NextJS would be valuable given the commitment to NextJS in our web ecosystem in general, allowing us to trivially fulfil data loading requirements via async server components for example.

In our Vite case, the pre-built HTML elements include the static content, the React root node (the hydration binding point), script tags (that makes the root node interactive) and everything else necessary for fully-interactive server-rendered content (e.g. style elements). Simply inlining the HTML elements (e.g. with dangerously set inner html) creates an interactive microfrontend. Can this be done with NextJS? How?

### Additional information

_No response_

### Example

_No response_
Next.js can’t really be “mounted” into an arbitrary DOM node the way a Vite/React app can, because Next’s runtime assumes it owns the whole document and hydration boundary for the route. In the Pages Router it hydrates `#__next` and expects that to correspond to the server-rendered document structure; in the App Router it still assumes it controls the document layout for the route. If you inline the HTML of a Next-rendered page inside some other host document and then load the Next client bundle, React compares what it expects vs what it finds and you get the “hydration mismatch → replace content” behavior you observed.

There isn’t a supported config option to say “hydrate only inside this arbitrary element and ignore the rest of the body”. Next is designed as the top-level app for a route, not as an embeddable widget.

What does work, depending on what you’re trying to achieve:

1) iframe (most reliable microfrontend boundary)
If you truly need to embed a Next “page” inside another page without interference, an iframe is the clean isolation boundary: separate document, separate hydration, no DOM ownership conflict. It’s boring but it works.

2) don’t embed a “page”; embed a “widget”
If you want a microfrontend-style island, build it as a standalone React entry (or a Next app exported as a widget) rather than trying to reuse a Next route. In practice that means:
- create a component/widget package
- render it into a known root (like Vite does)
- optionally fetch data from a Next API route / RSC endpoint / your backend
Next can still be part of the ecosystem (API, auth, data fetching), but the embedded thing shouldn’t be a Next “page”.

3) use module federation / separate build + host integration
Some teams do this with Next + webpack module federation or “remote components”, but it’s still not “inline SSR HTML then let Next hydrate it”. It’s usually “load remote JS and render into a host root”, and you lose the full Next page/document model.

4) server-side “include” without client hydration
If the goal is just to inline server-rendered HTML (for content) and you don’t actually need it to hydrate as a Next app, you can treat Next as an SSR HTML producer and include the HTML in the host page. But the moment you try to boot the Next client runtime against that markup inside another host document, you’re back to the ownership/hydration mismatch problem.

So the direct answer to your question:
- no, Next doesn’t support “explicit React root node binding for a page” as an embed target
- inlining a Next page’s SSR HTML into another document and then hydrating it “like Vite” is not a supported pattern
- if you need a fully interactive microfrontend, use an iframe or build a widget entry that hydrates into a dedicated root node (outside of Next’s page runtime)

Hi, amirhakim
Next.js is a framework built on top of React that gives you routing, data fetching, and server-side rendering out of the box. It still uses React components, so your React knowledge transfers directly.
​

What Next.js adds on top of React
File-based routing: pages are just files in app/ (or pages/), and the folder structure becomes the URL, so you don’t need React Router.
​

Multiple rendering modes: server-side rendering (SSR), static site generation (SSG), and client-side rendering (CSR) per page, which helps with performance and SEO.
​

How to think about it as a React dev
You still write components the same way, but you also decide where they run: server components (default in app/) or client components (with "use client" at the top).
​

Data fetching often happens in server components or route handlers instead of useEffect, which reduces client bundle size and avoids loading spinners everywhere.
​

Minimal mental model for a new Next app
app/layout.tsx: common layout (e.g., <html>, <body>, navbars) that wraps all pages.

app/page.tsx: your home page (/ route); export a React component from here and it becomes the main page.
​

Creating app/about/page.tsx automatically gives you the /about route without extra config.
​

Recommended learning path
Step 1: Skim the official “React & Next.js basics” pages (components, props, hooks, then “What is Next.js?”).

Step 2: Build a tiny app with:

app/page.tsx (home), app/about/page.tsx (second page)

A shared layout and a simple <Link> between pages.

Step 3: Add one data fetching example (e.g., server component using async to fetch data) so you feel the difference from useEffect-based fetching.

What is the role or UseEffect in React?

`useEffect` is used to **run code after the screen updates**.

### In simple words
> When React finishes showing something on the screen, `useEffect` lets you do extra work.

### Common uses
- Fetch data from an API
- Listen to events (scroll, resize)
- Start a timer
- Clean up when leaving a page

### Simple idea
> **Render UI first → then run `useEffect`**

Read this for more info: https://react.dev/reference/react/useEffect
Hi, Misyukka
Using `useEffect` in React allows you to run side effects after a component renders. A "side effect" is anything that affects the outside world, other than evaluating JSX. This includes things like fetching data, setting up subscriptions, and manually updating the DOM.

Key Idea
`useEffect` runs a function after React updates the DOM, keeping rendering pure and decoupled from side-effect code.

React re-runs the function based on the provided array of dependencies, allowing you to control when the effect runs (on every render, once, when a specific value changes, etc.).

Common Use Cases
Fetch data from an API when a component mounts or when a parameter (e.g., an ID) changes.

Subscribe to and clean up event listeners, WebSocket connections, or timers.

Syntax and Dependencies
js
useEffect(() => {

// Where the side effect occurs

return () => {

// Optional cleanup

};

}, [deps]);
